newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian PM squeezed between rebels, president.
newsitem.headline: Albanian PM squeezed between rebels, president.

text.p: Albanian premier Bashkim Fino is being squeezed between a hostile president and parliament on the one hand and rebels in the south who are refusing to lay down their arms as he strives to restore order in the country.
Handed the thankless task of pulling the country out of the armed chaos that gripped it for weeks, Fino faces an uphill task as he negotiates a minefield of Balkan party politics.

He is ruling a country divided between rebels in the south who are armed to the teeth with looted weapons and are calling for the resignation of President Sali Berisha, and a nervous north where civilians are just as heavily armed.
Fino scored an early success with an emergency bill to restore law and order on the anarchic streets by establishing highly-paid hit squads to disarm civilians who looted weapons from army depots.

But his attempt last week to bring the state radio and television under control of the multi-party interim government he heads was blocked by parliament, currently responsible for the media, which is firmly in the hands of President Sali Berisha's Democratic Party.
"I can't see Fino getting anything major through parliament before the elections," one Western diplomat said.

Fino's national reconciliation government was appointed earlier this month to restore order in the country and organise new elections by June. Berisha's Democrats won polls last May by a landslide, but they were condemned as seriously flawed by international observers and boycotted by the opposition.

There is a widespread belief that this summer's elections will be won by the main opposition Socialists, Fino's party, who are the reformed heirs of the hard-line communists that ruled Albania for over 40 years.

The rebels blame Berisha for not stopping shady pyramid savings schemes that operated for over three years before they collapsed in January, wiping out the life savings of thousands of families, particularly in the more prosperous south.
Even in the north, which has traditionally supported the president, a northerner by birth, and where losses in the failed schemes have been less significant, support for him appears to have waned.
Diplomats citing reliable sources say that up to 40 Democratic members of parliament have turned against Berisha, seeing him as an electoral liability.
Berisha himself has pledged to step down if the Democrats lose the election.
Fino, while clearly irritated by Berisha's blocking tactics, had made it clear he wants the president to stay in office until the elections.
"The government has a more important mission than asking for the president's resignation," Fino said on Saturday. "It would create an institutional vacuum if he were to resign."

Fino appears determined to restore public faith in the democratic processes, which was sorely tried by last year's questionable elections and Berisha's re-election by the tainted parliament earlier this year.

Moving cautiously but purposefully, Fino appears to have persuaded the rebels to drop their threat to set up a rival leadership in the south unless Berisha quits and await the outcome of the elections.

"Fino is working very well, he listens to everyone and he is very neutral," commented one member of parliament from the Monarchist Party, normally at the opposite end of the political spectrum to the ex-communists.

The toughest task is likely to be persuading ordinary Albanians to hand back the hundreds of thousands of weapons they seized from army depots in a wave of anarchy last week, which now present a constant threat to law and order.
Many diplomats believe the only solution is to buy them back, with money from abroad.
According to diplomats the government has already given a visiting European Union delegation a very detailed list of requirements to reequip the demoralised armed forces.
"Among other things they asked for 20,000 forks and spoons, but only 1,000 knives," one European diplomat said. "Maybe they were afraid of them falling into the wrong hands."
